edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De resurrectione carnis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.locus: On the Resurrection of the Flesh XVII
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Simplicior quisque fautor sententiae nostrae putabit, carnem etiam idcirco repraesentandam esse judicio, quia aliter anima non capiat passionem tormenti seu refrigerii, utpote incorporalis: hoc enim vulgus existimat. Nos autem animam corporalem et hic profitemur, et in suo volumine probamus, habentem proprium genus substantiae, soliditatis, per quam quid et sentire et pati possit. Nam et nunc animas torqueri, foverique penes Inferos, licet nudas, licet adhuc exules carnis, probavit Lazari exemplum. Dedi igitur adversario dicere: Ergo, quae habet corpulentiam propriam, de suo sufficiet ad facultatem passionis et sensus, ut non egeat repraesentatione carnis. Imo eatenus egebit, non qua sentire quid sine carne non possit, sed qua necesse est illam etiam cum carne sentire. Quantum enim ad agendum de suo sufficit, tantum et ad patiendum. Ad agendum autem minus de suo sufficit. Habet enim de suo solummodo cogitare, vel cupere, disponere; ad perficiendum autem operam carnis exspectat. Sic itaque et ad patiendum, societatem carnis expostulat; ut tam plene per eam pati possit, quam sine ea plene agere non potuit. Et ideo in quae de suo sufficit, eorum interim sententiam pendit, concupiscentiae, et cogitatus, et voluntatis. Porro, si haec satis essent ad plenitudinem meritorum, ut non requirerentur et facta, sufficeret in totum anima ad perfectionem judicii, de his judicanda, in quae agenda sola suffecerat. Cum vero etiam facta devincta sint meritis, facta autem per carnem administrentur; jam non sufficit animam sine carne foveri, sive cruciari, pro operibus etiam carnis, etsi habet corpus, etsi habet membra; quae proinde illi non sufficiunt ad sentiendum plene, quemadmodum nec ad agendum perfecte. Idcirco, pro quoquo modo egit, pro eo et patitur apud Inferos, prior degustans judicium, sicut prior induxit admissum: exspectans tamen et carnem, ut per illam etiam facta compenset, cui cogitata mandavit. Denique, haec erit ratio in ultimum finem destinati judicii, ut exhibitione carnis omnis divina censura perfici possit. Alioquin non sustineretur in finem, quod et nunc animae decerpunt apud Inferos, si solis animabus destinaretur.
thought_title: The Necessity of Flesh in Judgment
pass_a_gloss: Any simpler supporter of our opinion will think that the flesh is also to be represented in judgment, because otherwise the soul would not undergo the passion of torment or refreshment, since it is incorporeal: for the common people think this. But we, on the other hand, profess and prove in our own volume that the soul is corporeal, having its own kind of substance and solidity, through which it can both feel and suffer. For even now, the example of Lazarus has proven that souls are tormented and comforted among the dead, although they are naked and still exiled from the flesh. I have given the opponent the opportunity to say: Therefore, what has its own corporeality will be sufficient on its own for the capacity of passion and sensation, so that it does not need the representation of the flesh. On the contrary, it will need it to the extent that it is necessary for it to feel even with the flesh. For just as it is sufficient on its own for acting, so also is it sufficient for suffering. However, it is less sufficient on its own for acting. For it has on its own only the ability to think, or desire, or plan; but for completing its work, it awaits the flesh's operation. Similarly, therefore, it also demands the fellowship of the flesh for suffering; so that it can suffer as fully through it as it could not act fully without it. And therefore, in those things for which it is sufficient on its own, it hangs in the balance of its own opinion, of desires, and of thoughts. Furthermore, if these were enough for the fullness of merits, so that deeds would not be required, the soul would be sufficient on its own for the perfection of judgment, concerning those things that it alone would have been sufficient to do. But since deeds are also bound to merits, and deeds are administered through the flesh; now the soul is not sufficient to be comforted or tormented without the flesh, on account of the works of the flesh as well, even if it has a body, even if it has limbs; which, therefore, are not sufficient for it to feel fully, just as they are not sufficient for it to act perfectly. Therefore, in whatever way it acted, it also suffers among the dead, first tasting judgment, just as it first introduced the offense: yet still awaiting the flesh, so that through it also the deeds that it entrusted to its thoughts may be compensated. Finally, this will be the reason for the ultimate end of the destined judgment, so that the divine censure may be completed by the presentation of the flesh. Otherwise, what the souls now undergo among the dead would not be sustained in the end, if it were destined for souls alone.

pass_b_english: A simple-minded supporter of our view will argue that the flesh must also appear at the judgment because otherwise the soul, being incorporeal, could not experience the torment or refreshment of punishment — that is what the common people think. We, however, both profess and prove in our own treatise that the soul is corporeal, possessing its own kind of substance and solidity, through which it can both feel and suffer. Even now, the example of Lazarus has proven that souls are tormented and comforted among the dead, though they are naked and still exiled from the flesh (Luke 16:19-31). I have therefore granted my opponent this opening: "Since the soul has its own corporeality, it will suffice on its own for the capacity of sensation and suffering, so that it does not need the flesh to be represented." On the contrary, it will need the flesh precisely to the extent that it must feel even with the flesh. Just as the soul suffices on its own for acting, so it suffices for suffering — yet it is less sufficient on its own for acting. On its own it can only think, desire, or plan; to complete its work it awaits the operation of the flesh. In the same way, then, it demands the fellowship of the flesh for suffering, so that it may suffer as fully through the flesh as it could not act fully without it. Therefore, in those matters where the soul suffices on its own, its judgment hangs suspended over its own desires, thoughts, and volitions. Moreover, if those inner states were enough for the fullness of merits, so that deeds would not be required, the soul would suffice on its own for the perfection of judgment concerning the very things it alone could do. But since deeds are also bound to merits, and deeds are administered through the flesh, the soul is no longer sufficient to be comforted or tormented without the flesh — on account of the works of the flesh as well — even if it has a body and limbs. Those limbs, therefore, are not sufficient for it to feel fully, just as they are not sufficient for it to act perfectly. Consequently, in whatever way the soul acted, it also suffers among the dead, first tasting judgment just as it first introduced the offense, yet still awaiting the flesh so that through it the deeds it entrusted to its thoughts may be reckoned. Finally, this will be the reason for the ultimate end of the destined judgment: that the divine censure may be completed by the presentation of the flesh. Otherwise, what souls now undergo among the dead would not be sustained to the end, if judgment were destined for souls alone.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions regarding the soul's capacity for sensation and action versus its need for the flesh to complete its works. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source. The addition of the scripture citation (Luke 16:19-31) in Pass B is a required identification of the 'Lazari exemplum' and is correct.
